1.title: Know the parts of a computer and how it is made
1.intro: An electronic computer is made from boards, chips, memory, storage, power and a case. Learn the parts and the making steps.
pts: Name the main parts: processor, memory, storage, mainboard, power supply, cooling and case.
Explain what each part does in one sentence.
Explain the steps from parts to product: buy parts, build boards, assemble, test, pack.
Explain the difference between designing a computer and assembling one.
Name the main safety risk to parts: static electricity.
Sort the parts of a computer into bought, made in-house and software.
Draw the path of one unit through a workshop from the parts store to shipping.
1.ex: A small maker assembles desktop computers from bought boards and parts. They do not make chips. If bought parts cost 600 CAD per unit, a batch of 10 units needs 10 x 600 = 6,000 CAD of parts. Their value is choosing parts, building neatly and testing well.
1.act: Draw a block diagram of a computer with ten blocks and write the job of each.
1.std: Task: draw a computer block diagram. Condition: ten blocks. Standard: every block has an input, an output and a job, all correct.

2.title: Work safely with electronics
2.intro: Electronics work needs safe habits for people and for parts.
pts: Use an anti-static wrist strap and mat when you handle boards and chips.
Keep a clean, lit bench and store parts in labelled bins.
Use eye protection when you cut, solder or use compressed air.
Handle batteries with care: do not crush, short or heat them.
Check the current rules with the workplace safety board on training, ventilation and protective gear.
Store and carry boards in anti-static bags.
Practise a bench-end routine: power off, unplug, tidy tools and note any hazard.
2.ex: A new worker touches a memory card without a strap, so the batch of 40 units is flagged for extra tests. The tests take 2 hours, which is 120 minutes / 40 = 3 minutes per unit. The company adds a strap check at the bench door.
2.act: Write a one-page bench safety checklist and use it for a week.
2.std: Task: use a safety checklist. Condition: one week at a practice bench. Standard: each check is signed with a date and no unsafe step is skipped.

3.title: Know the rules for making and selling electronics
3.intro: Making electronics in Canada involves product, radio, safety and environment rules.
pts: Explain that electrical and electronic products often need approval by a recognised testing body before sale; check the current rule with the federal and provincial authorities.
Explain that devices that send radio signals must meet the federal radio rules; check the current rule with the federal regulator.
Explain that electronic waste has take-back rules that differ by province; check the local rule.
Explain that labels may need to be in English and French; check what applies.
Explain that selling abroad may need export permits for some technology; check before you ship.
Explain that products with a battery may have extra transport and safety rules; check the carrier and federal rules.
Keep a compliance file for each model with test reports, dates and label proofs.
3.ex: A maker plans to sell a mini computer with built-in Wi-Fi. The checklist shows radio approval and electrical safety approval are needed first. If the two tests run one after the other and take 3 weeks and 4 weeks, sales wait 3 + 4 = 7 weeks.
3.act: Build a rules table with rule, who enforces it, your product's status and the dated source.
3.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a dated source; nothing is guessed.

4.title: Assemble a board or a system step by step
4.intro: Assembly follows a written method so every unit is the same.
pts: Write a work instruction with numbered steps, photos and a torque or fit note.
Lay out parts in order and check them against a parts list before you start.
Install parts gently and check seating, cable routes and screws.
Mark each unit with a serial number and record who built it and when.
Do the first article check: the first unit is tested fully before the batch continues.
Build a jig or tray so every worker places parts the same way.
Time each step and add the times to find the time per unit.
4.ex: A work instruction for a ten-step build is tested with a new worker. She stalls at step six, so the photo is changed and the step is split in two, which makes 11 steps. If each step takes 3 minutes, a unit takes 11 x 3 = 33 minutes.
4.act: Write a work instruction and assemble two units from it.
4.std: Task: assemble two units. Condition: a written instruction. Standard: both units match, a second person can follow the steps and each unit has a record.

5.title: Test, find faults and improve yield
5.intro: Testing proves a unit works. Faults give the facts to improve the process.
pts: Write a test plan: power on, boot, memory check, storage check, ports, heat, run time.
Run a burn-in: run the unit for a set time and watch for faults.
Log each fault with unit, test, cause and fix.
Compute yield = good units / started units.
Fix the top cause first and test again.
Explain first-pass yield and final yield and why rework can hide problems.
Keep a defect chart that ranks causes by count.
5.ex: Of 50 started units, 43 pass at first test. Yield = 43 / 50 = 86%. The 7 failures are 4 loose memory seats, 2 bad cables and 1 other. A new seating check is added and the next batch reaches 94%, which is 47 of 50.
5.act: Run a test plan on five units and compute yield and the top fault cause.
5.std: Task: test and measure yield. Condition: five practice units. Standard: faults are logged with causes and the yield sum is correct and checked.

6.title: Manage parts, suppliers and quality
6.intro: Missing or bad parts stop a line. Plan supply and check what comes in.
pts: Check incoming parts against the order and inspect a sample.
Keep a supplier list with lead times and a second source for key parts.
Set a reorder point = daily use x lead time + safety stock.
Keep spares for the parts with long lead times.
Record batch numbers so a bad lot can be traced.
Take a sample such as 5 of every 100 parts on arrival, test them and record any bad ones with the batch number.
Explain that a part can go out of production; plan a last-time buy or a replacement.
6.ex: Daily use of a part is 6 and lead time is 14 days, with safety stock of 20. Reorder point = 6 x 14 + 20 = 104 units. When stock falls to 104 an order is placed, and the safety stock of 20 covers a late delivery.
6.act: Build a parts list with supplier, lead time and reorder point for ten parts.
6.std: Task: plan parts supply. Condition: ten parts. Standard: reorder points are calculated correctly and a second source is named for the key parts.

7.title: Price the product and prove it pays
7.intro: A computer maker earns by margin on each unit after paying for parts, time and testing.
pts: Variable cost per unit = parts + labour + test + packing + shipping.
Margin = price - variable cost.
Fixed cost = rent, tools, insurance, software and approvals, paid whatever you sell.
Break-even volume = fixed cost / margin per unit.
Test the price with real buyers before you commit; talk to a licensed accountant about tax.
Include warranty returns as a cost in the cost sheet.
Compare your price with three similar products and write why a buyer would pick yours.
7.ex: Price 1,200 CAD, variable cost 780, so margin = 1,200 - 780 = 420. Fixed cost is 10,000 per month, so break-even = 10,000 / 420 = 23.8, which rounds up to 24 units a month. At 30 units the monthly profit is 30 x 420 - 10,000 = 2,600 CAD (teaching numbers only).
7.act: Build a cost sheet, compute break-even and write what you would change if you were 30% short.
7.std: Task: price a computer. Condition: a spreadsheet. Standard: formulas are visible, three what-if cases are shown and a mentor checks the arithmetic.

8.title: Run a small production batch for real
8.intro: Run a pilot batch and measure it. Then decide to stop, change or grow.
pts: Set the batch size, schedule and a stop rule before you start.
Record yield, rework and time per unit each day.
Do a final check and pack with a care and warranty note; check the current consumer rules for warranties in your province.
Handle returns by reason and fix the top reason.
Write a 12-month plan with milestones, a budget and a risk list.
Write the stop rule as a number, for example yield below 80%.
Hold a short daily meeting to check yield, rework and parts.
8.ex: A pilot of 30 units reaches 90% yield, so 27 units pass, and takes 3 hours per unit. The stop rule was yield below 80%, which would be fewer than 24 good units. The decision is to run a second batch of 50.
8.act: Run a pilot batch of at least 10 units and write the review.
8.std: Task: run a pilot. Condition: a written plan and stop rule. Standard: measures are recorded daily, the review reasons from evidence and a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: Name four main parts of a computer.
Processor, memory, storage and mainboard (also power supply, cooling, case).
Why use an anti-static strap?
Static can damage chips and boards.
What is a first article check?
A full test of the first unit before the batch continues.
How do you compute yield?
Good units divided by started units.
How do you find a reorder point?
Daily use times lead time plus safety stock.
Why record serial and batch numbers?
So a bad unit or bad lot can be traced.
What may you need before selling a radio-enabled product?
Federal radio approval; check the current rule with the regulator.
What is break-even volume?
Fixed cost divided by margin per unit, rounded up to whole units.
What should you do with electronic waste?
Follow the take-back and disposal rule in your province.
What should you do if you are unsure of a rule?
Ask the official body or a licensed adviser and keep the answer in writing.
